title: Sorted Sets
subtitle: Leaderboards, rate limiting, and range queries
author: KERNAL

whyItExists.problem: Many features require ordered, ranked data: leaderboards, rate limit windows, priority queues, autocomplete, and time-based queries. Building these with sorted arrays requires O(N log N) re-sorting on every update.
whyItExists.solution: Sorted Sets maintain member-to-score mappings in a skip list. ZADD is O(log N), range queries are O(log N + M). The score-ordered structure makes real-time leaderboards and sliding-window rate limits trivial.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Leaderboards, rate limiting with sliding windows, priority queues, time-series range queries, autocomplete prefix indices.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: If order doesn't matter, use a Set (simpler). If you need insertion-order access, use a List.

explainModes.beginner: Sorted Sets are like a scoreboard where each player has a score and players are always ranked from lowest to highest. Add a player with a score, ask for the top 10, or find where a specific player ranks.
explainModes.simple: Every member in a Sorted Set has a floating-point score. Redis always keeps members sorted by score. ZADD adds/updates, ZRANGE queries by rank, ZRANGEBYSCORE queries by score, ZRANK tells you a member's position.
explainModes.standard: Sorted Sets combine a skip list (for O(log N) sorted access) with a hash table (for O(1) score lookup). ZADD is O(log N). Range queries are O(log N + M) where M is the number of results. Use ZRANGE ... REV for descending order. ZRANGEBYSCORE and ZRANGEBYLEX enable score and lexicographic ranges.
explainModes.technical: The skip list is a probabilistic data structure with O(log N) insert, delete, and range. The hash table maps member → score for O(1) ZSCORE. For small sorted sets (≤128 members, ≤64 bytes/member), Redis uses a listpack encoding that's cache-friendly. ZPOPMIN/ZPOPMAX atomically pop the min/max element — perfect for priority queues.
explainModes.deepDive: Sorted sets enable the sliding-window rate limiter without Lua: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE removes old entries, ZADD adds the current timestamp as both key and score, ZCARD counts the window. This is O(log N) per request — far cheaper than SET/INCR with multiple keys. ZRANGEBYLEX implements autocomplete: add all indexed terms with score 0, then ZRANGEBYLEX leaderboard '[alice' '[alice\xff' returns all entries starting with 'alice'.

content.text: Sorted Sets store unique members, each with a floating-point score. Members are always returned in score order. They combine a hash table (O(1) score lookup) with a skip list (O(log N) range queries).

content.code:
# Add members with scores
ZADD scores 1500 "alice" 2000 "bob" 1800 "carol"

# Update score (ZADD is upsert)
ZADD scores 2200 "alice"   # alice now has 2200

# Get score of a member
ZSCORE scores "alice"   # "2200"

# Rank (0-indexed, lowest score = rank 0)
ZRANK scores "alice"     # 1 (second lowest)
ZREVRANK scores "alice"  # 1 (second highest)

# Range by rank (ascending)
ZRANGE scores 0 2 WITHSCORES        # bottom 3
ZRANGE scores 0 2 WITHSCORES REV    # top 3 (descending)

# Range by score
ZRANGEBYSCORE scores 1700 2500      # between 1700 and 2500
ZRANGEBYSCORE scores -inf +inf      # all members

# Count members in score range
ZCOUNT scores 1700 2500             # count in range

# Remove members
ZREM scores "carol"                 # remove one
ZREMRANGEBYRANK scores 0 1          # remove bottom 2

content.text: Sorted Sets implement a precise sliding-window rate limiter by storing request timestamps as scores. Only requests within the last N seconds count.
Use ZINCRBY instead of ZADD to add to a score atomically. This is perfect for vote counts, page view tallies, and leaderboard point additions.

questions.question: What command returns members of a sorted set by rank, highest first?
questions.explanation: ZRANGE key 0 N WITHSCORES REV returns members from highest to lowest score (reverse rank order). Without REV, it returns lowest to highest.

questions.question: Can sorted set scores be negative?
options: Yes, scores are double-precision floats and can be any value
questions.explanation: Scores are double-precision floating-point numbers, so they can be negative, zero, positive, or even infinity (-inf/+inf for range queries).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of ZADD on a sorted set?
questions.explanation: ZADD is O(log N) because Redis uses a skip list internally. The skip list keeps elements sorted, and insertion into a skip list is O(log N).

faq.q: Can sorted set scores be negative?
faq.a: Yes. Scores are double-precision floats and can be any value including negative numbers or ±infinity.
ZRANGEBYLEX returns members in lexicographic order when all members have the same score. It's used for autocomplete and prefix searches.

faq.q: How do I implement weekly leaderboards that reset?
faq.a: Create a key like leaderboard:2026-W45 with an expiry set to the end of the week. Each week gets a fresh key; old ones auto-expire.
